results.title: Addressing Bias and Fairness in 360Degree Evaluation Processes
results.content: # **Addressing Bias and Fairness in 360Degree Evaluation Processes**. Understanding bias in 360-degree evaluations is crucial in ensuring fair and accurate feedback for employees. According to a study conducted by the Journal of Applied Psychology, researchers found that biases can significantly impact the way raters evaluate an individual's performance in a 360-degree assessment. These findings highlight the importance of implementing strategies to mitigate bias in 360-degree evaluations, such as training raters on unconscious bias awareness and fostering a culture of diversity and inclusion within the organization. By addressing bias in evaluations, organizations can ensure that feedback is more objective and valuable for employee development and performance improvement. To combat bias effectively, organizations need to implement diverse review panels, encourage open conversations about bias, and provide specific guidelines for feedback to ensure fairness and accuracy in the evaluation process. A case study of a multinational company implementing feedback mechanisms reported a 15% increase in employee satisfaction with evaluation processes, highlighting the importance of incorporating these elements to promote fairness and upholding credibility in evaluations. Implementing anti-bias measures in 360-degree assessments is crucial to ensure fair and accurate evaluations of individuals. By proactively addressing biases and promoting a culture of fairness in multi-rater feedback systems, organizations can enhance employee development, engagement, and overall performance. Mitigating bias in 360-degree evaluations is crucial for ensuring fair and accurate assessments of employees. Research conducted by the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) found that 78% of organizations use 360-degree feedback as part of their performance evaluation process. To address bias in 360-degree evaluations, organizations should implement best practices such as rater training, anonymity, and diversified rater selection. A study published in the Journal of Management Development showed that providing training on feedback delivery and emphasizing the importance of objective assessments can reduce bias in 360-degree evaluations by up to 30%. In conclusion, addressing bias and promoting fairness in 360-degree evaluation processes is crucial for maintaining the integrity and effectiveness of such assessments. Moving forward, it is imperative for organizations to prioritize ongoing evaluation of their 360-degree feedback processes to identify and address any biases that may arise.

results.content: ## AI Bias and Fairness Audits: Ensuring Ethical and Transparent Artificial Intelligence. ## Introduction to AI Bias and Fairness. Recognizing and addressing these biases is essential to develop AI systems that serve all users fairly. ## What Are AI Bias and Fairness Audits? AI Bias and Fairness Audits are systematic evaluations designed to identify, measure, and mitigate biases within AI systems. ## Common Sources of Bias in AI Systems. ### Human Bias in AI Development. Fairness audits play a pivotal role in fostering trust between AI developers, organizations, and end-users. When AI systems are transparently evaluated for bias, it reassures stakeholders that ethical considerations are prioritized. ## Methodologies for Conducting AI Fairness Audits. AI fairness audits typically involve a mix of quantitative and qualitative methods. IBM’s AI Fairness 360 provides a comprehensive set of metrics and bias mitigation algorithms. ## Role of Explainable AI (XAI) in Fairness Audits. Explainable AI (XAI) plays a critical role in fairness audits by making AI decision-making processes more transparent. ## Challenges in Performing AI Bias Audits. Conducting comprehensive AI bias audits can be hindered by technical challenges such as limited access to proprietary algorithms, insufficient data transparency, and the complexity of machine learning models. ## The Future of AI Bias and Fairness Auditing. The future of AI auditing lies in automation and AI-assisted tools that can continuously scan for bias in real-time. AI bias and fairness audits are not one-time tasks but ongoing commitments to ethical innovation. ## FAQs on AI Bias and Fairness Audits. Bias detection focuses on identifying specific instances of bias within datasets or algorithms, while fairness auditing is a broader, systematic evaluation of AI systems to ensure they operate ethically and without discrimination across various contexts. ****How often should AI systems be audited for fairness?****. While it is challenging to eliminate all bias due to the subjective nature of fairness and limitations in data, organizations can significantly reduce harmful biases through diligent auditing, diverse data practices, and ethical AI design. ****What are the best tools for conducting AI fairness audits?****. ### AI Bias and Fairness Audits: Ensuring Ethical and Transparent Artificial Intelligence. * AI Bias and Fairness Audits.

results.title: Abstract B002: Fairness by Design: End-to-End Bias Evaluation for LLM-Generated Data | Clinical Cancer Research | American Association for Cancer Research
results.content: # Abstract B002: Fairness by Design: End-to-End Bias Evaluation for LLM-Generated Data *Free*. ©2025 American Association for Cancer Research. American Association for Cancer Research. *Clin Cancer Res* (2025) 31 (13\_Supplement): B002. Cohen; Abstract B002: Fairness by Design: End-to-End Bias Evaluation for LLM-Generated Data. **Clin Cancer Res** 1 July 2025; 31 (13\_Supplement): B002. We propose an approach that comprehensively evaluates data quality, and apply it in assessing subgroup bias in the context of extracting clinical variables. A LLM was developed to extract initial and metastatic (met) breast cancer (BC) dx and date from the electronic health record (EHR). For verification checks and replication, a LLM-curated BC cohort (N=935,240) was compared to a human abstracted cohort (N=56,861) from the Flatiron Health Research Database. Verification checks assessed how often pts received definitive surgery or radiation after met dx (clinically unexpected). To assess bias, we stratified performance by race/ethnicity (Latinx, White, Black) and age (<50, 50-64, 65-75, 75+). For initial dx, LLM performance differed by race/ethnicity with higher recall among Black (+4.7%, CI:2.7%, 6.7%) and higher precision among Latinx (+1.2%, CI:0.2%, 2.3%) compared to White pts. We saw similar trends in abstractor performance except for pts 75+, with higher recall among Black (+1.2%, CI:0.2%, 2.2%) and higher precision among Latinx (+2.3%, CI:0.9%, 3.7%) compared to White pts. Verification checks showed no variation by race/ethnicity or age, except among pts 75+ among whom we saw a higher rate of surgery after met dx (21%) compared to those with expected sequence (15%, SMD=0.22). Finally, OS from initial and met dx aligned between abstracted- and LLM-generated datasets, except for the Latinx group, where confidence intervals did not overlap for 5-year OS (LLM:0.71 CI:0.70-0.71; abstracted:0.73 CI:0.71-0.75), but absolute differences were small. Using Flatiron’s quality assessment framework enabled a nuanced evaluation of bias in EHR data curation. We observed small but present subgroup differences across both abstraction and LLM curation approaches, which may reflect clinical or documentation complexity.
